The Orchestrator Rebalancing System is a sophisticated work scheduling component that optimizes the order and bundling of AI agents to improve early wiki quality. The system operates through deterministic strategies that bundle multiple analysis agents per commit rather than processing commits sequentially by single agent types. This approach ensures comprehensive coverage of each code change before moving to the next, creating richer initial wiki content.

The rebalancing introduces several key improvements: analysis agents (code-change, narrative, security, technical-debt, pattern, dependency) are now bundled together per commit with code-change running first to establish base content, followed by specialized agents adding their perspectives. Meta agents (link, structure, quality, consistency) activate earlier - after processing 20+ commits or achieving 50% coverage rather than waiting for complete analysis. Synthesis agents (overview, project-overview, getting-started, writer) trigger at lower thresholds (8 pages instead of higher counts) to create structural documentation sooner. The system includes comprehensive testing infrastructure through mock LLM services and checkpoint tracking to validate that bundling works correctly, meta agents activate appropriately, and synthesis occurs at the right intervals.

The orchestrator maintains backward compatibility with optional LLM-powered decision making while defaulting to the improved deterministic strategies. Two utility scripts provide testing and demonstration capabilities: a test harness that validates rebalancing behavior with mock responses, and a wiki generation script that produces complete documentation with progress checkpoints and detailed analytics.

The Technical Debt Analysis Agent is a specialized component of the CodeWiki system that automatically identifies and tracks code quality issues in Git commits. This agent performs comprehensive technical debt analysis by examining code changes through multiple lenses including complexity, maintainability, duplication, and technical shortcuts. The agent leverages large language models to analyze commit diffs and provides structured findings with severity levels, actionable recommendations, and tracking of debt accumulation or reduction over time.

The agent integrates seamlessly with the multi-agent analysis pipeline, implementing the standard Agent interface with a dedicated `technical-debt` type. It processes commits by building detailed prompts that include commit metadata and diff content, then parses structured LLM responses to extract findings, debt levels, and recommendations. The agent maintains a sophisticated understanding of technical debt patterns including deep nesting (>4 levels), long functions (>50 LOC), magic numbers, TODO/FIXME comments, god classes, and missing abstractions. It tracks both debt introduction and debt reduction, making it valuable for monitoring refactoring efforts and code quality trends.

The agent automatically generates wiki documentation for significant technical debt findings, creating dedicated report pages for high or critical debt levels and maintaining an overview page that tracks hotspots and recommendations across the codebase. This provides development teams with persistent, searchable documentation of code quality evolution and actionable insights for technical debt management.

The CodeWiki ignore system provides selective file filtering for repository analysis, similar to how .gitignore works for Git. The system uses a .cwignore file in the repository root to specify patterns for files and directories that should be excluded from code analysis. This filtering is applied throughout the codebase exploration tools, ensuring that generated content, build artifacts, and other irrelevant files don't interfere with the analysis process.

The ignore system follows .gitignore syntax conventions, supporting glob patterns, directory patterns (with trailing /), and comment lines. It automatically merges user-defined patterns with sensible defaults like node_modules/** and .git/**, ensuring essential directories are always excluded. The system includes performance optimizations through pattern caching and integrates seamlessly with the fast-glob library for efficient file matching. All codebase exploration tools (read_file, search_files, list_directory) respect these ignore patterns, providing a consistent filtering experience across the entire analysis pipeline.

The testing approach emphasizes real service integration where possible, using actual file repositories and git services in tests, with only the LLM service being mocked to ensure deterministic and fast test execution. This hybrid approach provides confidence in system integration while maintaining test isolation and speed.

The CodeWiki system now supports `.cwignore` files for selectively excluding paths during repository analysis. This feature follows the familiar `.gitignore` syntax, allowing developers to specify glob patterns for files and directories that should be ignored when analyzing codebases. The system always excludes common paths like `node_modules/**` and `.git/**` by default, while allowing projects to define additional exclusions through a `.cwignore` file placed in the repository root.

The implementation uses the `fast-glob` library for efficient pattern matching and includes a caching mechanism to avoid re-parsing ignore files on subsequent analysis runs. The parser handles standard gitignore conventions including comment lines (starting with `#`), empty lines, and automatic conversion of directory patterns (ending with `/`) to recursive glob patterns (`/**`). While negation patterns (`!pattern`) are recognized in the syntax, they are intentionally not supported since the underlying `fast-glob` library's ignore option doesn't handle them effectively.

The `.cwignore` system is particularly valuable for CodeWiki analysis because it allows projects to exclude generated content, build artifacts, test fixtures, and other non-source files that would otherwise clutter the analysis results. This improves both performance and relevance of the generated documentation by focusing on actual source code rather than derived or temporary files.

This approach ensures that getting started guides contain accurate, real-world information like actual npm scripts, verified file paths, and current project dependencies rather than generic or outdated instructions. The system implements an agentic tool interface that enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to autonomously explore codebases during wiki generation. This capability allows AI agents to read source files, search for patterns, and understand project structure beyond just analyzing existing wiki content. The implementation provides a foundation for more accurate and comprehensive documentation generation by granting agents direct access to the underlying codebase.

The agentic tool system consists of three core tools: `read_file` for accessing individual files, `search_files` for pattern-based file discovery, and `list_directory` for understanding project structure. These tools are integrated into the LLM service layer through a `completeWithTools` interface that manages multi-round conversations where the LLM can request tool executions, receive results, and continue processing until it has gathered sufficient information to complete its task.

The Project Overview Agent serves as the primary implementation example, using these tools to read README.md files, explore package.json dependencies, and examine source code structure to generate comprehensive project overviews. This represents a significant shift from purely reactive documentation generation to proactive codebase exploration, enabling agents to produce more accurate and contextually rich wiki pages by understanding the actual implementation rather than relying solely on commit messages and existing documentation.
